title: This used to be a computer.

notes.point: This used to be a computer.
notes.story: Introduce the event: Drink & Discover, MyWorkLounge, Friday 20 November 2026. In 1949 NACA staff transcribed flight recordings and used slide rules and electric calculators to reduce data to engineering units. Calculation required skilled people, equipment and time. Electronic computers later automated much of this work.

title: When calculation became cheap
body: Human calculation → Electronic computers → Interactive spreadsheets

notes.story: These were distinct developments: electronic computers automated calculation; VisiCalc, released for Apple II in 1979, brought interactive business modelling to ordinary business users. We did not just calculate the same things faster: scenarios, forecasts, budgets and sensitivity analysis became practical to explore. Cheaper technology can expand demand. Screenshot is a later capture, not a launch photograph.
notes.transition: Next: The world wants more software

title: The world wants more software
body: “the world wants a gigantic amount more software, hundred times, maybe a thousand times more software.”

notes.story: Sam Altman, Federal Reserve conference, July 22, 2025, transcript page 19. This is speculation, not a measured forecast. Why more software? Perhaps millions of small specialist workflows, personal applications, automations and niche business tools rather than only large consumer apps.
notes.transition: Next: App Store submissions reviewed: +49% since 2022

notes.story: Exact counts: 2022: 6,101,913; 2023: 6,892,500; 2024: 7,771,599; 2025: 9,100,620. Growth is 49.1%. Includes updates and resubmissions, not distinct new apps. This shows increased submission activity, not that AI caused growth. Internal tools, scripts, web apps and personal automations may never appear in an app store.

title: What becomes worth building?
body: An idea that wasn’t worth three months of development might be worth three afternoons of experimentation.

notes.story: A rhetorical illustration, not a factual estimate. Consider gym logging, specialist guitar editing, kitchen inventory and meal planning, or automating repetitive business work. These examples illustrate possibilities, not claims that every project exists. AI lowers the cost of experimentation; good products still require judgment. Start with the working personal gym application.

title: An impressive result is a beginning

notes.point: An impressive result is a beginning
notes.story: Explain why generating code is different from delivering software. Review and judgment catch incorrect assumptions, bugs and inappropriate abstractions. Good products still require problem definition, product judgment, design, architecture, integration, testing, security and ongoing maintenance.

notes.story: Don’t start by asking what you can build. Start by asking what would be worth building.
